name: SNAP food benefits
coverage: Screens Texas households against the published SNAP maximum income limits, the separate-household and categorically-eligible 165% column, and the older-adult or disability exception path. Deductions, work, student, residency and other non-financial rules are not screened here.
limitations: This is a partial income screen, not an agency determination.
Deductions are not calculated, so a household above the gross limit can still qualify after deductions.
Work, student, citizenship and other non-financial rules are not checked.
The published limits change on October 1 each year; the encoded table is effective October 1, 2025.
eligibilitySummary: SNAP helps with the cost of groceries and is run in Texas by Texas Health and Human Services.
Whether you qualify depends on who buys and prepares food together, your income and allowable deductions.
Households that include someone who is older or has a disability are measured differently and have extra pathways.
Texas HHS makes the final decision after reviewing your application.

evidence.text: The SNAP maximum income limits effective October 1, 2025 list gross monthly (130%) limits of $1,696 for a household of 1, $2,292 for 2, $2,888 for 3, $3,483 for 4, $4,079 for 5, $4,675 for 6, $5,271 for 7, $5,867 for 8, $6,463 for 9 and $7,059 for 10, plus $596 for each additional person.

The same table lists net monthly (100%) limits of $1,305 for a household of 1, $1,763 for 2, $2,221 for 3, $2,680 for 4, $3,138 for 5, $3,596 for 6, $4,055 for 7, $4,513 for 8, $4,972 for 9 and $5,431 for 10, plus $459 for each additional person.

The 165% column ($2,152 for 1, $2,909 for 2, $3,665 for 3, $4,421 for 4, $5,177 for 5, $5,934 for 6, $6,690 for 7, $7,446 for 8, $8,203 for 9, $8,960 for 10, plus $757 each additional person) is used to decide whether a person who is elderly or has a disability living with others may claim separate household status, and is also the income limit for categorically eligible households.

The handbook lists deductions used in the SNAP budget, including a standard deduction of $209 for households of three or fewer, $223 for four, $261 for five and $299 for six or more, a standard medical expense of $170 minus $35, a homeless shelter standard deduction of $198.99, a maximum excess shelter deduction of $744, a standard utility allowance of $445, a basic utility allowance of $400 and a telephone standard deduction of $62.

The monthly allotment is calculated from the household's net monthly income and household size: net monthly income is multiplied by .30, rounded up to the next whole dollar and subtracted from the maximum monthly allotment for that household size.
Texas benefits applications are submitted through Your Texas Benefits, which allows applying with an account or without one.

The Texas HHS SNAP overview page could not be reviewed on September 19, 2026 (HTTP 403), so no required document list is claimed here; the agency states which information applies to a specific household.

The encoded income limits and deduction amounts come from Revision 25-4, effective October 1, 2025; SNAP limits are adjusted annually on October 1, so the table must be re-checked before October 1, 2026.
Income limits are only part of SNAP eligibility; this screen does not check work, student, citizenship or other non-financial rules, which Texas HHS applies when it reviews an application.

value.text: The amount depends on your household and income.
